utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Colonel, may I remind you of the affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about an order or a combat report that was sent by Colonel Mrksic to the 1st Military District on the 20th of November at 6.00 in the evening, and that was at tab number 30. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before we finished you mentioned or you read out what Colonel Mrksic said to the 1st Military District about the taking over of the hospital on the 19th of November. Do you remember reading that out, that first paragraph? Sorry, it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Paragraph 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, it states that the hospital was taken over at 1000 hours. Do you know which -- which unit took over the hospital, which formation? On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report indicates that this task had been completed by 1100 hours on the 19th. As far as I remember, the hospital was taken by the 2nd Battalion of the military police, or at least some of its elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were any of the assault detachments that you had mentioned earlier, were any of those assault detachments involved in the taking over of the hospital on the 19th as well, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please pause a moment? Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend. There's something that needs clarifying. Were there any assault detachments on the 19th of November; I think that is a crucial issue. Given that the question is leading, and I think it requires a little more caution or perhaps some preliminary questions preceding this potentially leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I don't see it as you do. Clearly the witness has spoken earlier of assault detachments in various parts of the town of Vukovar or -- and here he is simply asked, you've mentioned those detachments earlier, were any of those involved in the taking over of the hospital on the 19th. It would be wasting time to go around and try and get him to think about assault detachments. Please carry on, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear that question about assault detachments?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it was elements of the 2nd Battalion of the military police that actually entered the hospital. I think a security system for the hospital was set up by that same unit. Immediate contact with the hospital was also established by some or all of Assault Detachment 1. They were in the -- in and around the hospital. They were certainly positioned around the hospital. I think that the unit that actually entered the hospital was the 2nd [realtime transcript read in error "1st"] Battalion of the military police, and I think that men from Assault Detachment 1 actually stayed just outside the hospital. That's what I believe to have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting. I think there is a mistake on page 3. We're talking about the 2nd Battalion of the military police, not the 1st.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance, just in case I misspoke, I'm talking about units of the 2nd Battalion of the military police. I hope I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It appears twice, once as the 2nd Battalion and then some lines later as the 1st Battalion. So you meant the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just to remind us, Colonel, who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time it was Major Radoje Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, after Colonel Mrksic reports about the task of taking over the hospital, he further discusses some problems in relation to the evacuation and transport of the civilian population on the 19th. If I can ask you to read, read out the section in relation to those problems, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 19th of November, 1991 measures were taken for the pulling out, evacuation and transport of the civilian population and those members of the Ustasha forces who were captured. This was done in an organised manner. We encountered great difficulty with the handover of civilians that were sent back to the Republic of Croatia at one of the barricades along the main road. The Croatian authorities refused to have them, so they were eventually returned to our zone in the evening hours. This created additional difficulty as far as the evacuation on the 20th of November, 1991 was concerned. During the selection, transport and handover of the prisoners of war, everything was done in keeping with the Geneva Conventions on POWs. Measures were taken to strengthen the command and control system to reinforce order and to increase discipline in the units. Activities were started to clear the mines, clear the terrain, as well as to clear the battlefield and pull out any damaged equipment and material and send it to be repaired."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the 20th of November, if we look at the second paragraph, further problems are discussed by Colonel Mrksic or reported in relation to the evacuation of the civilians, wounded and sick. Can you read that section out, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 20th of November, activities previously begun to clear the liberated territory and buildings from Vukovar from the remaining Ustasha forces continued and measures were resumed in order to establish full control of the town. The focus in terms of the clearing was on the settlement of Mitnica. During the clearing itself we came across large mined areas and booby-traps which made clearing the mines additionally difficult. We also encountered great difficulties while carrying out our tasks of evacuation and transport of civilians as well as the wounded and sick. Those civilians who were returned from the main road yesterday were returned several times again today from an agreed place of handover in the area of Nustar. The same thing happened with the civilians from the Velepromet area who were also returned several times. When another handover was finally agreed for 1500 hours the same problems occurred again. We agreed for the entire transport to be sent to Sid, since there was no other choice. The transport carrying the wounded that was supposed to be sent back to the Republic of Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, if I can stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document. It's tab 30, 65 ter number 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 421, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can now turn to tab 31, please. It's 65 ter number 192. And this is a report and order from Operational Group South command which the name Colonel Mrksic appears at the base of the report, and the time is 21st -- 21st of November at 6.00 in the morning. And it's an order relating to the issue of resubordination and the return of home units. Do you see that order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The signature at the base of the order, is that the signature of Colonel Mrksic or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the -- on the 21st of November, 1991, do you know where Colonel Mrksic was, what his activities were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st. Is that the date you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, and my recollection in turn is based on what I entered into the war diary, it should be as follows: At 0815 hours on the 21st, Colonel Mrksic is on his way to Belgrade to brief the federal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that entry, Your Honours, is at page 41 of the war diary. And that's Exhibit 401.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, how long was Colonel Mrksic away from Vukovar? Did he return that day or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did he return?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the afternoon of the 22nd. You can see his original signature on one of these orders, the 22nd, 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll have a look at that in a moment. But in relation to this order signed under the name of Colonel Mrksic, if we look at the first paragraph it states that in the course of the 21st of November, 1991, withdraw the Leva Supoderica volunteers detachment and place them, resubordinate them to the 12th -- and perhaps if you can state the unit that it was placed or resubordinated to, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20 -- the 12th Mechanised Brigade of the 12th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this resubordination occurred during the course of the 21st of November, is that correct, from what the order states?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether this was actually carried out is not something that I can say. That's what the commander's order says. It was supposed to be completed by 2400 hours on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said it's supposed to be completed by 2400 hours on the 20th or the 21st?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the 21st of November, withdraw the detachment and dispatch them to the 12th PMBR. So that means it was supposed to be done in the course of the day, the 21st of November. The commander of the Leva Supoderica detachment had to do as ordered. Perhaps he reported at sometime that he had not been able to; I don't know. I don't know whether he actually implemented this order by the dead-line. From a purely military point of view, he would have been expected to. Had he not been able to, he would have been expected to report so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So as of the 21st of November was the Leva Supoderica still under the subordination of Operational Group South? Under the command, I mean.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In actual fact, it could have been by 2400 hours on the 21st, or 0000 hours, no more, on the 22nd. But the paragraph itself seems quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So is your answer yes or no, that it was still under the command of Operational Group South, as of the 21st?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 21st, yes. The answer is yes. Preparations were carried out to send them to the 12th Corps. It reads: "In the course of the 21st, dispatch" -- which means prepare. Until it is dispatched. So the answer is yes, on the 21st. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Also in the order it's ordered that the Vukovar TO units be resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you see that at paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And similarly, based on this document, as of the 21st of November, 1991, is the Vukovar TO still under the command of Operational Group South or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were under the command of Operational Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this order was sent to the commander of the Seseljevci volunteers unit. Is that correct? Do you see that at base of the order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you able to say which unit that referred to? Does that unit have another name?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Leva Supoderica unit. Since members of Seselj's party were members of the Leva Supoderica unit. So it was often the case that this alternative name was used in documents. Seseljevci. The volunteer detachment, that's consistent. Volunteer is consistent, and detachment is consistent. The only thing that is not consistent is Leva Supoderica, but rather it says Seselj. And since I was the one who wrote this, maybe I was at the time led by the fact that this other name was often used, and maybe I told the recording clerk to use this name in writing the actual document. It may as well have been a typo. I really can't say. What I can say is that this must be in reference to the Leva Supoderica unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the commander of that unit was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, Lancuzanin. Lancuzanin. Nicknamed Kameni.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Kameni translates as stone face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was sent also to the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Motorised Battalion, yes. Yes, it was sent to the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the interpreter could not hear the last part of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion was Tesic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why was this order sent to Commander Tesic, as well as Kameni? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, given the fact that the Leva Supoderica detachment was part of the 1st Assault Detachment, this had to be also sent to the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment. The fact that it was sent to the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion doesn't say specifically the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, because this detachment is now leaving and this in itself may be an indication that once these units have left, the assault detachment itself may be disbanded altogether. At least it will cease to exist as a combat unit, which was originally set up to carry out a very specific task. I'm not sure if you get my meaning. So if this detachment leaves and based on the order they were supposed to leave by the 21st. In point of fact from the 22nd, at 0000 hours, the assault detachment ceases to exist and all that is left is the motorised battalion, which actually constituted the mainstay of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document, 65 ter number 192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 422.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can now turn to tab 32, which, in fact is 65 ter 68 but it's now previously become an exhibit, Your Honour, and the exhibit number is 368. Witness, if we look at this document, it's a report to the 1st Military District command, and again at the base of the report the name of Colonel Mrksic appears as commander of Operational Group South, and it's dated the 21st of November at 6.00. If you can look at the signature at the base of that report, and are you able to say whether or not that is or is not the signature of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's Colonel Mrksic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated earlier that on the 21st of November Colonel Mrksic went to Belgrade. On that day who was left in command in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether, in fact, he signed those -- this report and the previous order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical that he signed it. I can't remember. But I was the one to process the documents and as such it was my duty to take it to him for signature, if he was there. I could not have taken it to anyone else, and no one else would have signed this document other than him, because they were not authorised to do so. I cannot definitely say whether it is his signature or not, I can't remember, but it would be logical that that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at this report at paragraph 2 it discusses the transportation of civilians to Sid and Sremska Mitrovica, and also discusses the wounded being transported to Sremska Mitrovica during the 20th and the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that this report relates to the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital, or to other evacuations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded who were transferred to Mitrovica in the night between the 20th and the 21st, they could have been from the hospital, but they could also have been from other parts of town. The question is, why go to Mitrovica. I assume, and in some previous reports it stated that there were many problems about an agreement for surrender, probably everyone was being sent to Sremska Mitrovica until the exact place of surrender was determined. After that, it says that they were sent to Bosanska Raca. They could have been from the hospital but also from other parts of town because wounded later were also found in other sectors of Vukovar, in buildings and in certain other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals, not a large number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that it's very unclear, in relation to which evacuations this report is referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, evacuation is not mentioned here. What is mentioned here is transport. Transport would be the logical continuation of a previous action, which could have been an evacuation, separation, and preparation of people for transport, as well as preparation of the means to be used in the transport. People who were brought out from the hospital, from other parts, were subject to this matter of transport. Transport where? Transport to -- as to how the authorities agree to do it. Operations Group South had a lot of problems because the superior command and the organs of authority could not agree on these questions with the Croatian side. That's why they were all kept. So I think that when we're talking about this report on the 21st, I think that the bulk of the problems was resolved concerning the captured people who had weapons who were transported to Mitrovica, and then when we're talking about this probably last transport of the wounded to Mitrovica and then to Bosanska Raca, and then also when we're talking about the transfer of civilians, women and children to Sid. I think that that's when it was all completed, in the night of the 20th and the 21st, and also in the course of the 21st, as it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in terms of command responsibility in the military rules and regulations that existed, when a commander leaves his zone of responsibility, does his duty, does his -- do his responsibilities cease in relation to the activities occurring in the area, or do they continue if he chooses to leave for any short period of time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we concluded in relation to the rules that were in force at that time, the responsibility of the commander cannot be distilled. If he is absent, then there is a person who is allocated to stand in for him. In this case it would be the Chief of Staff. He is responsible for all that goes on, even when he is absent as commander. So this is this objective responsibility of each commander. For his unit, for his zone and for his operation. Subjective responsibility would be the responsibility of the person who carries out or does not carry out tasks assigned to him in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the responsibility continues from -- for the commander that has left to ensure that the military rules and regulations and the combat duties are being adhered to appropriately in his zone of responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He has the right to take all the measures in his capacity as commander if duties are not being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is an exhibit already, so that doesn't need to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, if we could turn to tab 33, please. That's 65 ter number 591. And it's a combat -- this is a combat report from the 1st Military District command dated the 21st of November, 1991, military number 1614-178. And it's signed by Major General Vujovic. If you can look at the conclusion, please, and in relation to the paragraph that directly precedes it, if you could read that paragraph out, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this combat report is sent to the first administration of the General Staff. "Conclusion: Enemy activities on the line of contact and in the depth lead to the conclusion that" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, Colonel, if I could stop you there. Perhaps if I could ask you to read out the paragraph above where the major general reports that prisoners were strictly -- the conduct was strictly in accordance with the Geneva Convention, so if you could read that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Captured enemy forces are being processed, selected and sent to processed as printed, points, according to plan. Work with and conduct towards the prisoners are strictly in conformity with the Geneva Conventions on prisoners of war. "As part of the assignment on the set-up of commands in liberated areas, units are encountering several problems: Certain groups of locals, 'volunteers' and others independently undertake activities which are not in line with the situation or the decisions of the military command."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, thank you. Now, the 1st Military District covers the area of Operational Group South; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of Operations Group South is part of the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District. It's in their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And with the problems that Major General Vujovic was mentioning, were you aware of those problems occurring in Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While treating the prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, in that matter I was informed that there were no problems except for small incidents which occurred in the areas of the Assault Detachment 1 during the evacuation in the places where they were billeted. This is my personal information, and it's based on what I heard in the operations room, that there were considerable difficulties, that members of local TO forces were trying to mistreat these people. There were also cases of physical assault, but there were no serious consequences. Other than that, I don't know anything else about violations of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the prisoners. I didn't hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic. Sorry to interrupt, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As usual, it's an intervention for the transcript. It's page 15, line 17, I think that the witness said that there were problems during evacuation until they arrived at the places where they were billeted, but in the translation it says that there were problems during evacuation in the places they were accommodated or billeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, perhaps you can clear that up. Thanks, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, if we can discuss some more about these problems and incidents that you heard occurring, and it's unclear at this stage whether you stated whether you -- you heard those incidents occurring in the places where they were billeted or from the place where they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you think that I'm not clear, at certain intervals I heard some of these things, and I heard that there were problems to secure them by members of the JNA during the evacuation or I can call it transfer. Because we're talking about the relocation of the sick, but we had wounded here, women, children. So in the actual transfer along the roads from the hospital sector and from the other parts of town where they were being taken from, in that period when this was practically going on, there were problems in the problems where they were billeted in the same way. Attempts by people to enter into the buildings where these people were placed, there were curses, this kind of verbal type of assault as well as minor physical assaults. I meant both the one and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I'll just -- will read an entry that was placed in the war diary by you on the 20th of November at 7.00 in the morning. And the English is at page 41. Perhaps if you can look at the war diary for the 20th of November at 7.00 in the morning, please. Sorry, that's in tab 10, that's Exhibit 401.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20th of November, 0700. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can read that entry out, and then I'll ask you some questions about it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander of Operations Group South regulated and ordered the implementation of activities regarding the mopping up and control of the territory." Then: "Evacuation and the transport of civilians from Ovcara and Velepromet and the Vukovar Hospital (order strictly confidential number 439-1 of 20th of November, 1991)."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And to your knowledge at that time, at 7.00 in the morning on the 20th, were there civilians or people held at Ovcara, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I wasn't there. But I stand by what is written here because the commander was quite precise. Evacuation and transport of civilians from Ovcara and Velepromet, yes, they were there on the 20th. And the Vukovar Hospital probably. Yes, on the 20th. On the 19th in the evening it was agreed with Dr. Vesna Bosanac to carry out the evacuation of the hospital. And it was carried out on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to be clear, the date that you -- the day that you said that you heard -- you had heard problems with the way people were being treated, in relation to the evacuation and the places where they were billeted, what date was that? What date are you referring to when these problems occurred? Is that the 20th or some other date?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were problems on all three days. On the 18th in Mitnica, but these were minor problems which are quite realistically possible in such a situation. I heard about the 19th too, that there were problems regarding the transport or the transfer of people from the captured parts of town, primarily from the central part of town to Velepromet, the barracks and Ovcara. That there were problems with the local population as well as members of the Territorial Defence who are from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I had already explained the mistreatment. All that time this abuse was of the same intensity. There was verbal abuse as well as physical assaults, but they were not of a serious nature and did not result in major consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And so for those three days, the 18th, the 19th and the 20th of November, where were you largely based? Were you at the headquarters or were you out in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the command post all three days. In the operations room when I was working, and at the time when I had my planned rest I was in the building that we used for rest. I wasn't there continually, but during those three days I was most often at the place where I was carrying out my regular tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can take your mind back to the 19th of November at the headquarters, you mentioned that you heard problems of verbal abuse and physical abuse at places such as the Vukovar barracks and Ovcara, and you stated that the local population and the Territorial Defence were causing the problems. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this question by my learned friend is leading because the witness said that there were problems in the transport of people from the captured parts of town to Velepromet, Ovcara and the barracks, while my learned friend is asking whether there were such problems at Ovcara, at the barracks, and this is considerable difference, whether that's on the way to those places or in those locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also said that there was physical abuse and the witness did describe the forms of that abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel, you were about to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I cannot mention the term "transport" that Mr. Vasic mentioned now in any context, other than when we're talking about an organised activity to transfer people from one building, from one area, by means of transport, to another location. Here I mentioned the terms "evacuation" and "relocation" or "transfer" and I think that I was clear. I did not mention transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, is there anything further you would like to follow up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Not on that particular point, Your Honour. I think he's clarified it. However, the topic in general, there are some further questions about the nature of the abuse, et cetera. And perhaps, because it's very short, close to the break, perhaps I could start after the break. Sorry, Your Honour, I am -- I came to court at 9.00 this morning, no one was here, and so I'm on that time-frame. So I'll continue. I suppose better half an hour early than half an hour late.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to that, the problems that you talked about with the local population and the Territorial Defence, what types of reports were you receiving on the 19th? How were those reports coming in? And I'm talking about the 19th now, not the 20th.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports by the commanders were something that I didn't really follow up in that sense. To be specific, I did hear reports by senior officers in the organs of command who, at that time, on the 19th, were at the units of operation -- the operations group in those places where these things were happening. Amongst other things, I think that on the 19th, and also on the 20th, the Chief of Staff was at the scene and he was busy with matters relating to the transfer. I think -- the evacuation, and I heard that from him. So the situation was that the commanders would go, then they would come back in the middle of the day, eat something, and then go back again. So each one of them would say something, but it wasn't really that much that they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in relation to the 19th, is your evidence that you were hearing problems of this nature at each of the three places you mentioned at Ovcara, at Velepromet and at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I was then the head of the operations, I didn't know the time precisely, and I can't be any more precise now, how people were separated and who were sent to Velepromet, who was sent to the barracks or to Ovcara. I simply know that they were sent to all three locations, but according to what criteria, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether on the 19th other of the command staff at the headquarters were familiar with these problems as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all those who were there, who stayed there for short or extended periods of time in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was Colonel Mrksic aware of these problems on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. And that he knew more about the problems. He was told about the problems by the commanders of his subordinate units and by the Chief of Staff, I would presume, as well as the head of security and other officers within the command who were sent to Vukovar where all this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the head of security in the command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of security was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the 19th, was any action taken to try and prevent this verbal abuse and physical abuse from occurring at these locations? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that on the 19th at 2000 hours a group came to the command at Negoslavci. They were from the security organs of the 1st Military District and the General Staff. They were received by the commander. And, as far as I can remember, they were tasked with dealing with evacuation and transfer, as well as some other issues that may occur at a later stage in the transport of those people. I believe they remained at the command for a brief period of time, and having told Mr. Mrksic why they were there, he sent them to the area of Vukovar to complete their tasks. And during the night, between the 19th and the 20th, around midnight, another group came from the rear, from the logistics. They were from the 1st Military District. Most of them were there concerning the traffic in order to regulate that matter in the area. And they were to carry out their tasks together with the rear services of the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can we talk about the first meeting when a group came from the 1st Military District and the General Staff to the headquarters of Negoslavci. And this is the meeting that you stated occurred at 8.00 on the 19th, in the evening. Were you present at that meeting, or were you just aware of it occurring in the -- in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be specific. I was present, the commander was present. I don't know whether there was someone else from any other organs of the command, perhaps another person or a couple of them. And the meeting was held, those people came in, they introduced themselves, and they described their tasks. The commander understood why they were there. They only wanted to know where exactly was the area. He provided them with some escort, and he sent them out in the field to deal with those issues. There wasn't much discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Approximately how long did that first meeting last? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to object to this question by my learned friend. I believe the witness said that there was no meeting, but on page 22, line 18, it states that there was a meeting, but I believe the witness said something to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, in the English translation the witness is describing a meeting in that part of the transcript. Perhaps instead of you going over it again the witness might just confirm. Can you see in the transcript at 22 an answer commencing around line 19 and extending much further down. Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a meeting. Depending -- that depends on the point of view. In the true sense of the term, a meeting deals with issues, it has an agenda, it is chaired by someone, it lasts longer. This was a brief encounter. Perhaps I may have said a meeting, but in Serbian we don't make the distinction. Temporal duration is not specified either. A meeting is attended by several people. But this was basically the meeting of the commander with people from the security organ. I happened to be there, and perhaps another couple of people. We didn't participate in any discussion, we didn't put forward any suggestions or anything of that sort. I didn't really think this definition of "meeting" through. I may have used the word "meeting," but this was an encounter, as I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps -- just to clarify: How long did this meeting or encounter, how long did it last for? Are we talking minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very brief. It lasted 10 to 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did it occur inside the headquarters or outside?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the command building. At least the meeting that I was present at, that took place in the operations room. Whether they met in front of the building or later on in some other place, that I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that some individuals from the 1st Military District had come to the headquarters. Do you know any of their names?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know anyone from the group that came from the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many came from the security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific. More than three, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to command staff that were present, you mentioned yourself and Colonel Mrksic. Was there anyone else from the command staff there, and particularly the security organs present from Operational Group South command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Colonel Mrksic there and myself. Apart from the two of us, I don't remember whether anyone else was there. I presume there was someone from the security organ, it is something to be expected, since our counterparts came from the security organ, but I am uncertain as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When this -- when meeting was taking place, do you know where Major Sljivancanin was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time. I can't be specific. I know he used to spend his time with the units, most of his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. The duties of the security organ, the individuals from the security organ from the 1st Military District, what were they? Did they say why they were there and what they were going to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember concerning security, they said that they were to see what the situation was, how POWs were being treated, as well as what the situation was with the wounded and civilians, and to take the measures necessary to help carry out the process in a planned and organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did Colonel Mrksic give them any instructions or, if not, how did he respond to this? Especially in relation to how prisoners of war were being treated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Colonel Mrksic's response; I didn't note that down in my notebook. Since they left for Vukovar quite soon, I believe he explained them how to get there and that they would be escorted by someone and that they could see the situation in the field for themselves. And I believe that on the 19th he told them there were no problems, and that Mrs. Vesna Bosanac had been there before they came and that things were arranged. I don't know what their tasks were. I don't know or I don't remember having them stated, those tasks, precisely to Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. However, were the problems in relation to the minor physical assaults or abuse at Ovcara, Velepromet and the hospital, and the verbal abuse, were they raised with these men?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the second time, our learned friend is trying to suggest asking whether the problems occurred at all three locations, and the witness only spoke of those problems the way to Ovcara and the barracks and at Velepromet. He never mentioned the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have another objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic. I think you are more accurate. My note about the hospital is dealing with a slightly different subject. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If that's the case, I apologise, Your Honour, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, with the problems at Ovcara -- sorry. Another objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let this be clarified first, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, were the problems that you heard about were occurring at Ovcara and Velepromet on the 19th, were they raised with these men from the security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, is there now something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not anymore, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned that there was another meeting or encounter later that evening, quite late. Was it with -- at the headquarters, was it with the same men from the security organs, or others?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. I believe this is a leading question. I believe the witness mentioned the meeting with the rear units from the 1st Military District rather than security organs. The witness stated that they came to the barracks in the evening and he never mentioned any meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake there, Your Honour. Perhaps if I can ask the witness just to clarify what that second meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What the second group were there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't got to a meeting yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I hope we do, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, a little more care, perhaps, Mr. Smith, with your questions. There have been a series of objections, and they're all because of loosely framed questions by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, did anyone else come to the headquarters after that -- after that first meeting with individuals from the security organs? And if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1.00 on the 20th, and that is no longer the 19th, a team from the logistics organ of the 1st Military District came. Their task was to deal with the rear -- issues of the rear transport primarily. They came there upon request of the command of OG South to assist, since they had the means which the Operations Group South didn't have. They had their tasks to carry out, and as far as I can remember they were linked up with the responsible officer of the rear services of OG South. And there was no meeting at the command; they came separately. I presume they had a meeting with the rear services, and they were briefed there on the situation and on how to deal with the issues they were supposed to resolve. So there was a meeting or an encounter. They arrived there, but I don't know whether they were seen by Colonel Mrksic or Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. Since they were from the logistics, they were sent to see the people from the logistics of OG South. So I would call that an encounter rather than a meeting, as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that they came on the request of the command to assist. In particular, in practical terms, what types of things were they requested to assist with?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the command of OG South did not ask specifically for certain things, but based on the documents of the superior command, which instructed that in case of problems they should seek assistance, they did so. I believe the OG South, in a document, requested assistance from the rear services of its superior command. There were several reasons for that. One of them being the supply of food for all the people who were in the area during those two or three days. The other reason being to regulate transport as well as to secure that transport. Those were the main issues that had to be dealt with by Operations Group South. And later on they were dealt with by the rear services of the operations group, together with the rear services of the military district. As to the degree of their success in doing so, well, that's another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that encounter, was there any discussion about the evacuation of civilians or people from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they came with someone from the village of Berak, from the rear organ. Or maybe someone from the rear organ was there waiting for them and then they started discussing the specific issues. I don't think the commander was familiar with their tasks in detail. He had the competent organs, and he forwarded them to -- forwarded them to the rear services, so as not to waste his time. I mentioned that another group came from the security organ in the evening. Therefore, the 1st Military District was trying to assist in dealing with the problems that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did those individuals from the security organs that arrived at the headquarters earlier in the evening, did they return later that night or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know for how long they stayed or when they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And now, perhaps, if we can move to the 20th of November, I'd like you to explain when you first heard about these problems of physical and verbal abuse at Ovcara and Velepromet. You mentioned that you heard of these problems over the three-day period, on the 18th, 19th and 20th, but now I would just like to draw your mind to when you first heard about these problems on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th, around noon, and during the afternoon, I heard there were some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who did you hear these problems from?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the officers there who came and then returned to the combat area. And by that time that was the liberated area in Vukovar. As someone from the command, I never received an official report by any commander. I don't know whether such a report was received by the Chief of Staff or the brigade commander, but we could hear from all the officers who were there that there were problems, that the conscripts and the JNA officers had great difficulty to deal with the members of the TO and civilians from Vukovar to prevent them from maltreating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many officers were informing you and others of that, of these problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember all that. It was on the 19th, or to be more specific, on the 20th, during which time most of the brigade command officers had to have been there at a certain point. In the operations room, there were only people who were there according to their routine tasks. That is, the duty officer, someone from the operations organ and someone from the staff. For example, heads of branches. Everyone else was in the field. And they occasionally came to the command for various reasons, and they all stated a similar thing, that it was very difficult to keep at bay members of the TO and civilians from Vukovar, so as not to maltreat people the way I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's now 11.00, so it may be time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, before we had the break you were talking about the problems that you heard from other officers at the command headquarters in relation to abuse of evacuees. You stated that the problems -- you first started to hear of these problems around noon, and in relation to the 20th, around noon on the 20th. For what period of time were these reports coming in, in relation to the day of the 20th, these reports of abuse of evacuees?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. I'm not sure if -- I'm sorry. I'm not sure if my learned friend is using the right word, "report." I think perhaps it would be better to have the witness explain himself whether these were actually reports or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are wanting to read "reports" in one particular context. It has a much more general meaning where this is a reliable usage. You might be sitting in the front foyer of this building as lots of people walk by and you heard reports of what was happening outside the building as they talked, as they went by. So I think we will allow it in Mr. Smith's favour on this occasion that he's using "reports" in that sense. Clearly the evidence so far does not support the notion that officers walked in the door and made a formal report. You heard enough there, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had to work hard for you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I much appreciate it. I think a 50/50 success rate on objection is not bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, how was this information conveyed by the other officers in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No official reports on these problems arrived, not to my knowledge. If they were official and if they did arrive, it is possible that they came straight to the commander, possibly to the Chief of Staff, if he was there, and indeed he was there, and he was also on the ground. I personally received no report from any of these subordinate commanders. There was a degree of information flow, if I may call it that, in that room. Sometimes there were more people present, sometimes not so many people. This was information coming from the officers who were there and whose assignment was to go, see what the problem was about and tackle it. Not all at once. And the scope itself wasn't too broad really, but it was about this, the Territorial Defence units, the local population were obstructing work, were making things difficult, were aggravating this large-scale problem with a large amount of people being transferred from Vukovar to these other areas that we have mentioned. What this means is the information flow was regular and anybody should have taken note. If problems had been more serious, if anybody had been murdered, each commander would have been duty-bound to draft a final report and forward it to their command. And then the commander would have known. I would have known. Any of the officers there would have known, had this been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But in particular, in relation to the information you received regarding the abuse of evacuees on the 20th, was that brought to the attention of Colonel Mrksic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he was aware of that or indeed that he wasn't. In his capacity as commander he would have had to know more than I did, for example, concerning the information that I was receiving. If you want me to explain that from a military perspective, whenever there is a serious problem in a unit this needs to be reported straight to the superior officer. If there were any serious problems, the subordinate officers were duty-bound to report on those and tell the superior officer. If they didn't, then there was no reporting. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was Colonel Mrksic at the headquarters on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The -- the reports in relation to the -- these informal reports in relation to the treatment of evacuees, can you say whether that was well known amongst the command staff on the 20th, and additionally on those other days, the 18th and 19th, from your observations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say, "Almost everybody," is there any person that you know didn't know this information?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was explaining about who exactly was going on -- was going about their own assignments in that operations room, you must have realised that the entire staff was there. As to when each of them were or were not there at which precise point in time, well, that varied. Who might not have been familiar, the logistics people, the security people who weren't really spending that much time in the operations room there, they were spending much more time out there in the field. But if they were spending so much time out in the field, then I suppose the inference would be that they must have known a lot more than we knew back in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to Colonel Mrksic, on the 20th was he -- do you know where he was? Was he mainly in the field or mainly at headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember about Colonel Mrksic's whereabouts on the 20th at the headquarters leads me to believe, at least based on what the war diary seems to indicate on the 21st at 8.15, he was on his way to see the federal secretary about the assignments that he had been given. He gave me the assignment to draw up a chart of how the Vukovar operation was carried out. And this was to include a number of accompanying documents, calculations, casualties and problems in general. I was supposed to prepare this chart for him so that he would be able to bring it to the briefing, and that was the assignment that he gave me. This assignment was tackled by certain officers from the operations organ. It was going out into the field, and there were one or two of them helping me with this assignment that I got. I did this that afternoon and the first half of the following night, between the 20th and the 21st. I was greatly aided in this by Colonel Pavkovic, who is an expert in this sort of thing. He's very good at drawing maps and producing maps. On that day Colonel Mrksic, if what I remember is correct, and if what is noted in the war diary is correct, in relation to the 21st, was at the headquarters. Late in the afternoon or early in the evening, at one point he left the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if I could stop there.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he went --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if I can just stop you there. You state that on that day Colonel Mrksic, if what I remember is correct, in relation to the 21st, he was at the headquarters. Do you mean the 21st or do you mean the 20th? Because in the war diary the entry is that Colonel Mrksic left at 8.15 on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to be accurate. I'm talking about the 20th. I mentioned the 21st in the context of what I remember, and what the war diary indicates, that he left on the 21st. And this brings me back to the 20th when, objectively speaking, there was little time for me to do all these things. So the situation I was facing was that I had to work quickly, I had to seek assistance, specifically from Colonel Pavkovic. There was a need to deal with this quickly, get the documents ready for the briefing, and this was done on the afternoon of the 20th and the first half of the following night. Colonel Mrksic was not around as those documents were being drafted. He was present at the headquarters during that day while there was still natural light. I just didn't see it fit that I should go to him and ask him for help about this. I was just drafting all those auxiliary maps that were necessary for Operation Vukovar. When he left eventually, late in the afternoon or early in the evening, Colonel Pavkovic turned up and he helped me finish the map and all the other auxiliary documents. I later heard that Colonel Mrksic returned just before midnight. I informed him that I had completed my task and that I had finished the map. As far as I remember, he said, "It's all right. We'll not be looking at that now, we'll do that tomorrow morning." And then he went to get some rest. I later learned that he had either been in the medical room or with the logistics people that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to Colonel Panic, where was he on the 20th? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Panic was my superior, that's true. But he did not issue my assignments, nor did he tell me where to go. I did make a note in the war diary, and I see that he was there on the 18th and the 19th where the problems were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the 20th. Even if you didn't make a note about it, do you know where he was on the 20th? Can you say or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just briefly, you stated that the first information came in about these problems, came in on the 20th at noon. For about what period of time did these -- did this information come in? Was it over minutes, hours? Can you give us an idea of how frequent this information was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that question. Whenever an officer turned up they would normally say something. "I'm tired." "We're facing a lot of problems over there." Some said, "I'm tired. There were some problems but we dealt with those." "Officers and soldiers are holding up just fine. The locals, the TO people, were stopped from doing anything bad, and were stopped from mistreating people." Those were the sort of comments made by most officers entering the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to Ovcara, the reports or problems from Ovcara, do you remember the names of the officers that provided that information or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Velepromet, the barracks and Ovcara were all the same to me. I did not have any information concerning the distinction criteria between those, which bodies were at Ovcara, which bodies were at the barracks and which were at Velepromet. Whenever I was told that something was going on in those respective areas, well, that was it, there something was going on. I wasn't necessarily asking myself whether that was at Velepromet, the barracks, or Ovcara. There was no need for me at the time to look into those matters. There was something going on all over the place all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Previously you referred us to an order placing Lieutenant Vojnovic, the town commander in Ovcara. Lieutenant-colonel, sorry. Did you see him on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. On the 20th of November I don't think I did. I saw Vujovic [as interpreted] at the brigade command three or four times. He would come there, I was present when -- well, for the most part he talked about problems, he made proposals, he was always unhappy about something or other. I realised he was an officer. He was not a -- a lieutenant-colonel or something like that, I don't remember the rank, but he wanted to prove his worth. He sometimes even ignored his superior. He was part of the Assault Detachment 1, and he would go straight to the command post. That was the sort of officer he was, and I wasn't prone to respect anyone who was of that ilk and I wasn't much listening to what he had to say either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, but now I'm just referring you back to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Did you hear any information --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I wasn't sufficiently focused on your question, perhaps. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It could have quite easily been my pronunciation. But in relation to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, did you -- even if you didn't see him on the 20th, did you hear anything about him on the 20th, about what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him on the 20th. I did not see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic at all during my time in Vukovar. All the information that I have, all the information that I'm aware of, is in relation to orders from the superior command about the resubordination of units, orders from our commander, the various assignments given to that unit in writing. I assume that there were oral orders being issued to him by the commander. But all I know is that he was the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade. I didn't see him on that day, I didn't see him on that evening. As for that evening, I think there was a meeting, or a briefing, you might say. He wasn't there. I do remember clearly, however, that later on, at about 2000 hours, possibly 2100 hours, I did hear that he had been to the brigade command; one of the officers told me. And he wanted to speak to Colonel Mrksic. I didn't investigate the matter, not then and not later. I never learned whether he had, in fact, met Colonel Mrksic and whether they talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Even though you didn't investigate the matter, did you hear what the subject of the discussion was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, I heard things off the record from officers. I heard that he had mentioned in their presence, in the presence of whichever officers those were who actually heard what he said, whether that's official, whether he actually met Colonel Mrksic and whether he told him is not something that I can talk about. But they said that he had been talking about problems, about mistreatment, about how the prisoners at Ovcara had been treated, specifically. By the same token -- as those prisoners who had been mistreated on one of the previous days, but he did mention that specifically and that's what I remember. There were some officers who apparently met him, saw him and talked to him, and apparently this is what he shared with them. I'm not sure if he told Colonel Mrksic about this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you hear this information on the 20th or at a later date?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th, on the 20th, the information, I got the information on the evening of the 20th, at about 2000 hours or 2100 hours, thereabouts. We were at the headquarters at the command and someone dropped a hint. I think it was Milorad Vojnovic. He wanted to see the commander. I'm not sure if he had met him previously or not, nor did people tell me. He said there are problems at Ovcara, problems with prisoners, and these problems have to do with the TO units there. And that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether Colonel Mrksic issued any orders to subordinates to protect prisoners at either Ovcara, Velepromet, or any other place on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he didn't. He didn't -- he didn't at that regular briefing actually raise the issue. There was no focus on that issue, nor were any assignments actually handed out. But command can be exercised by means of direct contact between people, and tasks may have been handed out in personal contact in the sense of punishing any acts that may have been committed. But at that particular meeting, which was actually a short briefing session, this problem was not mentioned specifically. As far as I remember, what was discussed is the fact that people were worn out and that the equipment was worn out. People were tired. What to do, how to get more things, how to get some rest, how to allow people to have some rest, and how to mend our equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Page 40, lines 11 and 12, it says there was a short briefing and this problem was not mentioned specifically. And the witness said this problem was not mentioned specifically in a drastic form. And this was not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, when you say that the problem wasn't mentioned specifically in a drastic form, how was it mentioned? In what type of form?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same form as information was received which I obtained from the officers I mentioned. There are problems, there is mistreatment, but everything is still under control and nothing extreme has yet happened. If that is so, then warnings might have followed, and calls for measures to be taken to keep anything extreme from happening. And these warnings probably did come from the commander or the Chief of Staff. I may have said a thing or two myself about that. Just in order to have this monitored, because this had been going on for three days. An assessment of the tendency of this thing to escalate could not have been made at the time unless there were reports, specific reports that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And to your knowledge, between the 20th of November and the 24th of November, when the Guards Motorised Brigade returned to Belgrade, were there any investigations or disciplinary measures taken against any soldiers involved in the abuse of evacuees or detainees on the 18th, 19th and 20th, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that any disciplinary steps were taken against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, can we now just briefly turn our mind to the evacuation of Vukovar Hospital? You have talked about it, and you have discussed aspects of it through the orders that were issued, and there was one order that you referred to that Colonel Mrksic drafted, or you drafted and he signed, which was very general, and that order was issued at 6.00 in the morning on the 20th. And that order didn't direct who was to organise or supervise the evacuation of people from the Vukovar Hospital. Do you remember discussing that order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital? Not the takeover of the hospital, but who was placed in charge to evacuate the people there? And especially the prisoners of war or the -- especially the combatants that were alleged to have been at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have inferred yourself, the order to evacuate was not specific. This means the implementing agent is not defined in the order, nor are there any criteria given in the order in terms of the place and time and the purely organisational aspects, and I mean the physical room in which the whole thing was taking place. So this was a pretty general thing. If you want me to say why the order has this general nature, I can tell you that this is my opinion. First of all, it was my belief that the security organs that we've mentioned, those from the 1st Military District, from the General Staff on the evening of the 19th, had this assignment: They were supposed to regulate, monitor and help. Part of this assignment was to be carried out by the logistics organs from the 1st Military District, including these same organs from Operations Group South. This issue should have been taken up by the moral-guidance organs. And by some kind of logic that was inherent in these things, the Chief of Staff should have dealt with these things. Why wasn't that written down, why wasn't that specified in detail, much in the same manner as I'm telling you now? Well, these are the reasons. And there is also the possibility that the commander ordered someone orally to implement this. And this person in charge of implementing this was an experienced officer. In that case, that officer would have got the whole thing organised pretty quickly, I think. So that, roughly speaking, is my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether Colonel Mrksic, in fact, did order someone to implement this? And if he did, who did he order to implement the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. All I said was that it was logical that he should have ordered someone. I commented on the order. It was written after the meeting with Dr. Vesna Bosanac. Some questions were discussed there. I wasn't present at that meeting, and Colonel Mrksic did not tell me exactly how to regulate that question. He didn't tell me anything specific, point this person as the responsible person, work out the organisation in the way you think fit, and then I will look at it. I didn't get anything like that from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it was your belief that the security organs of the 1st Military District and some general staff were supposed to regulate, monitor and help the evacuation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also stated --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that this was regulated by some order that I haven't seen. However, I think that sending a group of high-ranking officers to an assignment in the Vukovar zone of operations must have been regulated by an order, and that order must have contained specific tasks. This order has to be somewhere, and I guess that would clarify a lot of things; what was the assignment, did they have an assignment at all, and how were they supposed to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you -- you also said that the evacuation also included the same organs from the -- the Operational Group South. Are you referring to the security organs in operation -- the security organ in Operational Group South command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had to be included also. To what extent this was so, I really don't have the information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that, "He had to be included also." When you say "he," who do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the security organ. So I said "he"; actually, it was supposed to be "it." So the officers from the security organs should have been included. Included in the problem of resolving the relocation and the transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the command staff, who were the officers of the security organ in relation to OG South, Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise if I cannot remember everyone. I probably won't be able to remember them all. The chief was Major Veselin Sljivancanin. I don't know if it was the first senior officer or his deputy, but that was Major Vukasinovic. A captain was also there, a captain or a lieutenant, Borce Karanfilov. There were a number of non-commissioned officers, also a captain by the name of Mladen Karan. There was another officer whom I cannot remember, he was probably ranking immediately after the Chief, the number two man was Vukasinovic, perhaps number three person in that security organ, he was in Vukovar. This is what I remember. I mentioned that when I arrived at the guards brigade I really had to master the organisation and structure very quickly, I had to get to know the personnel quickly, and in those combat conditions, this is what I did. But I didn't find out about all the organs. The security organ in particular was not something that I really focused on. But the names that I mentioned, I think, were most of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a name of Mladen Karan, and unfortunately the last part of the name wasn't recorded in the transcript. Can you state that person's name again?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
