utterances.text: Mladen Karan, as far as I can recall. The first name is Mladen; the last name is Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a Captain Karanfilov as part of the organisational [sic] group south command staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Borce Karanfilov. Yes, I mentioned him, I know him. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was his function again?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisation of work in the security organ was something that I was not familiar. When I arrived, the principle was in peacetime that each of the officers in the security organ covers one or two units in the operations and security sense at the rank of battalion and light artillery battalion. Who of the officers was responsible for which unit is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Major Vukasinovic, and I think you also referred to him previously in your testimony in relation to an order by Colonel Mrksic assigning him to be a village commander, a village or town commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it -- is it a usual practice or a normal practice to place a security officer as commander of a -- of a particular region or zone?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, this was the local commander of the place where the command was located. The security organ is by organisation, a part of the command. Major Vukasinovic is in the security organ; therefore, he is a member of the command. So it is logical that he would appointed for that. It could have been any of the lower-ranking officers in the security organ too, but he was the one who was appointed and this seems quite all right to me. It would be wrong, but the commander could have made that decision to appoint Major Vukasinovic as the commander of Jakubovac, for example, but he appointed him as commander of Negoslavci. So it's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But before the appointment of Major Vukasinovic to this village or town command, did he have any authority to command people underneath him or subordinates underneath him, prior to his appointment as the town or village commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question, well, the security organs do not carry out functions of command. They are in charge of operations and security tasks, in the expert sense. Only in the expert sense they are superiors to the military police units. So Major Vukasinovic did not have the authority to have command of anything other than according to an order of the command in relation to Negoslavci when he was appointed as local commander, in terms of the questions indicated by the commander in the order and that we discussed. Therefore, he could not have been in command in any area, and if he did, that was something that was outside of his competence. Perhaps he just did this on the basis of his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: However, you say that he was appointed as a local commander by Colonel Mrksic. Does that mean he could exercise command powers as a result of that appointment or not? Command powers over subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the domain of what is defined in the order, local commander and the duties of a local commander are laid down. So he is responsible for this and this and this, and he is the indisputable commander who is, in turn, responsible to his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So that I understand it clearly, is it the case that normally Major Vukasinovic wouldn't have command powers, but Colonel Mrksic had the ability to vest command powers into Major Vukasinovic as a result of that order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade commander wanted and was obliged to regulate the setting up of military authority in certain sectors of the area of responsibility, and that is what he did. He covered the entire area of the zone of operations, assigning commanders to certain locations. Amongst them he appointed Major Vukasinovic commander of the settlement of Negoslavci and included him in the command functions in that sector, the sector of Negoslavci, in questions that are amongst the duties of local commander. Major Vukasinovic could not have commanded or interfered in the command duties of the local commander at Berak, for example, in these questions. But as far as this other aspect that I talked about, the operational and security aspect, these are some other duties in the ambit of the security organs that I'm not really very familiar with, and right now I couldn't say all that much about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it your understanding that the individuals from the 1st Military District, the security organs and others, that their role in relation to the evacuation was to assist Colonel Mrksic in it, or to organise it? Can you give us an understanding how that -- their role from the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If subordination was respected and the manner of command, then that group had to come with an order from the authorised commander and that order would define the time, the area, and the tasks. That order, I don't know whether they brought and showed that order to Mrksic. I know that that order did not arrive at the command in the regular channels, if it did not come, perhaps, through the command -- security organs of the command of Operations Group South. So in the order it would exactly state whether they had come to monitor it or to carry out the evacuation itself, to be mainly responsible for that or just to assist. But I don't know about this order. They could have had any number of assignments, one of the three that I mentioned. I cannot specify which one they actually did have, but I assume that they came to deal with the problems of the wounded, the captured, women, civilians, and women and children in particular, because that was in their jurisdiction, and then from the security aspect to evaluate the problems and to plan for any eventual positive or negative developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 48, line 22 states that they were dealing with the problems of the captured women, but I think that the witness only said problems of the captured. So I don't think that the -- what I see from the transcript exactly reflects what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to Major Sljivancanin, what was his role in the evacuation of people from the Vukovar Hospital; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his role was in the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital, and I don't know what his assignment was. I wasn't present at any time when he was being tasked by his commander. I did not write the order as an operations officer for the security organs to carry out any assignments in the zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to Major Sljivancanin's role generally, I think you've testified that you said that he was the chief, the chief officer of the security organ in the command staff of Operational Group South. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've also stated that the command staff or the security -- the command staff in the security organ have expert control -- not control, but expert responsibility for some units below. Is that correct? And I'm going to ask you to make it clearer. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately we have a classic problem here with the interpretation that we're constantly encountering and that I have discussed with the interpreters. The witness quite clearly said the word "expert control." This is what he said. I notice that in the English they are constantly using our word "rukovodjenje," as "control," so in that sense this interpretation by the Prosecutor as "control" which we also use in our language as "control" is not identical. I'm probably not being clear enough, but the witness is using a different word which is expertly used in the regulations as the term "rukovodjenje." I don't know how the interpreters are going to deal with this comment, mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What do you say it should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, when -- or the first day when documents were analysed with the witness, the word that was officially interpreted by the interpreters as the word "command" and the word used in -- was used in one of the translations was translated as "supervision" or "supervising." I'm not sure whether that is the right word. But the word "control" in our language and in English has a difference sense than the word "rukovodjenje." Perhaps some other experts in the courtroom will be able to differentiate and explain the essential difference in those two terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment it remains unresolved, Mr. Lukic. And we, as a Chamber, are in the hands of the interpreters. But you say, as you would understand it, that it is nearer the sense of supervision, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the official translation of the term "komandovanje i rukovodjenje" is command and control. This is the official term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I consulted the interpreters, they told me that the word "command and control" in the military sense from the aspect of Anglo-Saxon law is used as a term that is then incorporated in the translation of our terms, "komandovanje" and -- "i rukovodjenje." Perhaps we could officially address the translation service so that they can explain in the grammatical or the terminological sense that the word "rukovodjenje" is not the same as the word "kontrola" in our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In military sense, command and control makes a lot of logic. It makes sense. It involves supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it's quite clear to you why I am looking at this term a little bit differently from the aspect of the security organs who are exerting expert control. All I wanted -- well, I don't really want to make things complicated, Your Honours, but the -- the term that the witness got in English was the term "control," but he was using the term "rukovodjenje." So we will probably continue to clarify these terms in the course of the proceedings in their proper, strict meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a concept rather than a matter of strict meaning, and it's a concept that has to work in a military structure. You will -- it's been pointed out to me that the document which is before us in tab 3, which is the guidelines that became an approved text-book for command and control is using exactly the Serbian word that you are concerned about. And it's translated as command and control. I'm not sure that this case will turn on that issue. But, Mr. Lukic, if you can throw greater light on to it, please do so at some future time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, which units did the security organ or command staff of the security organ, which units did they have a responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the security sense or from that aspect they had a responsibility for all the units of the guards brigade, all the groups belonging to the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the military police. Did they have any specific responsibility for the military police or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not really that well-versed with -- in that area, but what I do know is probably correct. Units of the military police had an expert function, and these organs did have the authority as regards the manner of use of units of the military police in the conduct of tasks of an operational or a security nature. The use of units of the military police in combat operations was not something that was in their jurisdiction. They did not regulate or have the right to order them. All they had to do was to suggest this use to the commander, make suggestions to the commander. The use of military police units in combat is something that is regulated by a decision of the commander of the brigade or the commander of the operations group. Some specific tasks and assignments that I mentioned, such as expert supervision, the actual way in which activities were regulated in accordance with the authority of the police and the planning of these assignments was something that was in the domain of the security organs. However, use in combat was not in their domain. This is what I know. Perhaps this is not a competent answer in the expert sense, because I was never actually -- I never did anything in this -- this manner, this was not part of my regular duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And as was exemplified in the example you gave of Lieutenant Vojnovic who was placed as the village or town commander of an area, is it also possible for, say -- would it have been possible for Colonel Mrksic as a brigade commander or the commander of Operational Group South to place a -- an officer of the security organ in charge of a particular operation, whether it be a combat operation or an evacuation operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is always possible. It's always possible. Everyone is subordinated to the commander, so the commander could order the chief of the security organ to regulate, to prepare a proposal, and to submit it for his adoption, in terms of who would be the one amongst the officers to supervise this practically. So where we had the local or sector commander, such as Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, in that case an officer from the security organs could have and should have been sent there. And the particular time that we're talking about, and in any other time, when we're talking about the life, the work and the -- the implementation of combat operations, this would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can help us understand the role that Major Sljivancanin had and function he had when he was in Vukovar, what type of work did he do, from your observation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in practice, are you asking me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As chief of the security organ, his functions were clear, as well as his duties and tasks. He, I assume, carried out those functions, duties and tasks. As to how he carried them out, this is a matter of the assessment of the commander. He was always, practically every day, at the front lines of contact with the enemy as a senior officer and security organ senior officer, that was not his duty, but I think that this is something that is extremely positive and that had a positive motivational value, both on the officers and soldiers. Not only his presence, but the presence of other officers that the commander and the Chief of Staff sent there. His commitment to be there constantly was something that was up to him personally, but as a staff officer at the function that you know I was performing, I believe that this was something positive, and it's always a positive practice when you see something like this happening in the military. Secondly, not only from the motivational aspect, but he also advised and helped the commanders to resolve certain problems, and in the expert sense he probably resolved matters that had to do with security and operations matters that were in his domain. He was quite exposed in the media; he appeared in the media more than was objectively necessary. We watched that on television every evening. Whether this is something that he wanted or whether this was something that should have been like that, that is also something that concerns him personally. It's his thing, so it's up to him to judge that. As I said, Major Sljivancanin was present at meetings and the regular briefings at the OG South command. I viewed that again from the point of view that security organs always have something to tell the commander that not all the command organs should know. I don't know if he did have such contacts with the commander, Colonel Mrksic, and I don't know what their communication was in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, the previous question, I answered that I don't know whether he received any kind of duties or assignments in relation to the evacuation. I think that it is clear that those organs and -- are actually supposed to be used in this manner. That is all. He did not have the right, as I said, to command units of the military police. If there was any command and carrying out of orders, this was probably with the approval or agreement of the commander, and it was probably a result of the authority that he enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to Major Sljivancanin's active role in the field, in the operation in Vukovar, that would have had to have been with the approval of Colonel Mrksic. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, if I can now ask you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith. We've run six minutes overtime. I think we should now break if you're now moving to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a little after 25 minutes to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break you were discussing the active role that Major Sljivancanin had in the combat operations in Vukovar. I would like you to turn to the war diary, please; that's Exhibit 401. It's tab 10 in your folder, Colonel. And I would like you to turn to the entry on the 21st of October, at 4.30 p.m. It's page 30 in the English. Have you found the 21st of October at 4.30?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I was looking at November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, it's easier for the English speakers, because we have --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could read that entry in the journal, please, read that out.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Major Veselin Sljivancanin has informed General Panic that he corrected artillery fire in the Mitnica sector at about 1300 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what is your understanding of how a person corrects artillery fire? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corrections are made by artillery officers in keeping with the decision issued as well as according to the defined tasks. To be specific, we can talk about certain types of correction, depending on the type of artillery unit involved. That particular unit's commander corrects the fire, depending on the targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So in that sense, for a person, a military soldier or officer to be able to correct artillery fire, does that person need to instruct other people to do it? Is that, by implication, what that means, he's instructing other people?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the commander's decision and the targets, or objectives, the Chief of Staff puts together the list of objectives in keeping with the commander's decision. Before opening fire it has to be corrected, depending on the target, and the correction is made to confirm the actual outcome of opening fire. Provided this is the type of corrections they had in mind in the diary, then it is as I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Usually for an officer to be able to correct artillery fire, is it usual that that person has to have -- hold some sort of position of authority over the people firing the weapon, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any unit deployed at a firing position of any level, in order to open fire, has to be commanded by a commander. In B/C/S "komandir" or "komandant," up to the level of company or above. He corrects fire and no one else can do that. Based on the commander's decision, the list of targets exists, they are then being entered in the plan log of the artillery chief, and for that chief, in order to carry out the tasks issued by the commander, needs to do that in a precise manner. Before doing that, he needs to do the corrections. They fire a few shells to test the accuracy, and an artillery unit can comprise one weapon or several weapons trained on a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns who can do that, only the commander of the artillery unit. He has the plan given by the head of artillery, and then he makes the corrections. On occasions, some targets can be targeted without corrections, given the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But is it normal that a security officer has the ability to correct artillery fire in the context of the Vukovar operation? Was that normal?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most officers are able to do that; in particular, up to the level of lieutenant-colonel or colonel. But that concerns the issue of powers bestowed on any given commander, and I've already dealt with that issue before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And why is that information recorded in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see for yourself, any important information or event is entered. I believe Mitnica presented a problem at the time. That means that the Croatian forces were more active in that area, and that artillery fire was needed to deal with the situation. Provided I am correct, they needed to open up fire and it was done with the corrections or adjustments made by Major Sljivancanin. It wasn't one of his powers, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say how often Major Sljivancanin would be involved in this type of activity, correcting artillery fire, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered this in the log, I may have entered some others, I don't know. As regards this issue. But I can't say how often. Perhaps this was the only occasion, perhaps there were several. But not everything needed necessarily be entered into the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that Major Sljivancanin was in the media in relation to the combat operations in Vukovar. About how often was he in the media?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often. Whenever there was mention of Vukovar in the media, he was there. That is, I have in mind the television as it was then, the TV of Serbia or Yugoslavia, I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is this normal for security officers to be in the media speaking about combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Journalists will be journalists. An operations organ or security organ officer, such as I was, if asked something by any journalist, before I can answer I need to have a permission by my commander. Provided I have that permission, I will provide information. Therefore, one could do that, provided that person had the commander's approval. And I don't know whether he had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to talk briefly about the type of authority that Colonel Mrksic exercised in the Vukovar operation as commander of Operational Group South. Was he actively in the field, or was he more at headquarters? Can you give us an understanding of how he exercised his command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any commander that has reliable information on the situation and the development of combat activities in the area of operation commands from his command post. In order to have such reliable information, as we've discussed, we've also mentioned how to attain such information. That includes precise reporting, controlling the officers he sent, as well as going out in the field personally on the ground inside the zone. As regards that, he wasn't there quite often, so he didn't have this personal insight at all times. I believe the reports of subordinate commands and the reports of officers from the brigade command sufficed for him to manage the operation. And he was at his command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And when, say, problems arose in combat operations, any problems, would he -- would he delegate that to subordinates to deal with, or would he have an inclination to be involved in -- in those problems himself in resolving them? And perhaps we're talking about large problems here.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always reacted to significant problems, and he always set up his own mode of activity or type of reaction. A report by subordinate commander would usually be concluded with a question, being, "Could you deal with the problem based on the instructions I gave you. If not, I will send someone or I will appear there personally. If you can do that, then deal with the problem." In principle, that was the way used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to talk about Vojislav Seselj. Did he ever visit Vukovar whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him visiting Vukovar, and all officers knew about that. He was in Vukovar, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether he visited the Vukovar combat zone, or the Operational Group South zone on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of one such occasion. And I know he was in that part of the zone of operations that was close to the Assault Detachment No. 1 where the Leva Supoderica was. He wasn't at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And approximately what date that was, or what month at least?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific. It was at the very end of October or in early November. Perhaps the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of his visit was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His volunteers were there. I suppose he wanted to see them and to see for himself the way they behaved and what sort of treatment they received there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could he enter into the area of Operational Group South zone of responsibility without the authorisation of the operational group command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the effect of Seselj's visit to Vukovar? Were you able to monitor that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically. I didn't see anything. I suppose the presence of such an important leader of a party could improve the morale or provide additional information for the volunteers he sent there. It seemed to me that as regards their discipline his visit had a positive impact rather than a negative one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to Major Tesic, who you've testified was the commander of Assault Detachment 1, did he attend the daily meetings at the Negoslavci headquarters, the command headquarters of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he ever discuss the behaviour of the men that were assigned to his assault detachment, the behaviour of his subordinates in terms of discipline or lack of discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He frequently phoned in reports, reports talking about the problems he encountered while exercising command over his men. For the most part, these problems related to the Territorial Defence men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you -- or can you explain what type of problems he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of all it was about the dynamism of the realisation of the assignment that was set in relation to such orders and decisions based on orders that he may have received. There was little impact. He always wanted support. He always talked about the volunteers not listening to him. He always talked about the TO men not listening to him. There were always problems for him. I received these reports from him myself. He would phone me, and I would immediately inform the Chief of Staff and the commander. They would then take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when -- when you say that he talked about the volunteers not listening to him, are you thinking of any volunteer individual or groups in particular?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his report, and then you ask him what's the problem. Well, the volunteers, well, the TO men, they're not carrying out the assignments I give them in full, and that is why the dynamic implementation of the tasks in my area is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about lack of discipline in relation to protection of property, protection of civilians, protection of prisoners? Did you hear of those types of complaints from Major Tesic or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did mention that too, although less frequently. For the most part, it was about everything that he was responsible for in terms of carrying out assignments. That was the most important thing for him to report on, if it had to do with taking up a certain area that was specified in an assignment, but he often talked about breaches of discipline in his own unit. I'm saying most of all he talked about that. But he talked about the TO men and the volunteers in this context, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that he frequently phoned in reports talking about the problems. In addition to phoning in reports, were any of those problems raised at the meeting, the command meetings or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Always at command meetings. They weren't always problems. The operation itself took a long time. His task was a complex one. Sometimes for one or two days at a time things would go smoothly, and he would inform the commander accordingly, not that the situation was going according to plan in other parts of the front, and that's why the commander took the decisions that we have previously considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the commanders of other assault detachments that you've referred to, did those commanders have similar complaints about lack of discipline and motivation in their detachments or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the commander of Assault Detachment 2 did not refer to that kind of problem. He had a different one. His problem was the strength of the Croatian units in that area, along that axis. There was strong resistance from the fortified positions, and he couldn't cope with the dynamism that had been imposed on him. The same thing applies to the commander of Assault Detachment 3, at the outset, but later the same thing applied to other commanders too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In terms of problems of motivation and discipline, which assault detachment commander would have expressed the most problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of Assault Detachment No. 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your observations and from hearing these complaints, are you able to say why Assault Detachment 1 had more problems than the others? Was there a distinguishing feature about Assault Detachment 1 relative to the others or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the word go, this assault detachment comprised the Petrova Gora TO unit, not from the moment they arrived, but from the time the brigade command took over command of the operations group. So that was literally from the word go. And those were TO men from the area, from the area of Petrova Gora, and this area coincides with the area covered by Assault Detachment 1 and then further down the lines. From the word go, I suppose, the TO men expected or had their own ideas about how the operation would unfold. They probably had other expectations too. Be that as it may, that may have been one of the reasons why they were losing momentum and why there was a lack of motivation, which led them to cause all these problems. As for the other assault detachments, those were TO units that arrived at later stages of the operation from a variety of different sources. When they came for the first couple of days, there would be no trouble at all, as a rule. My opinion is that all these TO units, and especially when talking about Assault Detachment 1, were formally subordinated to someone, but what wasn't there, regrettably, was any kind of effective command over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the evacuations of civilians and combatants that you have referred to over the 18th, 19th and 20th of November, what was your view -- did you hold any view about the possibility of revenge attacks on people that were being escorted or evacuated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This amounts to being able to predict something. Being able to predict something is up to the command and everybody there. It was possible to foresee that the TO men and after the liberation, maybe even some of the locals who were not directly involved in the fighting, might try to commit acts of revenge in some way, or mistreat some of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, I would like you to turn back to one of the documents referred to earlier. And this is tab number 33, please. 65 ter number 591. And this is a combat report dated the 21st of November, 1991 signed by Major General Vujovic. Do you have that report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in that report, which commenced our discussion of undisciplined behaviour, et cetera, the major had informed that there was some problems with volunteers, et cetera, in the 1st Military District in terms of discipline. And at the end of that report there was a conclusion, and if I can read it to you. It states that: "Command will take the necessary steps to protect the civilian population from possible reprisals and misconduct by individual armed groups in their zones of responsibility." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion. It's not my place to pass judgement on a document drafted by my superior command. If this is a conclusion, then it shouldn't say the commands "will" or "shall" take the necessary steps, because at this point it becomes an order. The commands should take appropriate steps maybe with some reinforcements, with some more equipment, something could have been done to take protective measures. But regardless of that, although this appears to be an order, it is nothing, if not logical, measures must be taken, protective measures, and willful acts must be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender document 591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 423.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can now turn to tab number 34, please. This is a new document, not on the 65 ter list. The ERN numbers are 0463-8416 to 0463-8416, and the B/C/S is the same number. Witness, this is an order from Colonel Mrksic, Operational Group South zone commander, and it's dated the 22nd of November, 1991, and it's an order regulating the issue of the clearing up of the battle-ground.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who is the order addressed to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the staff commander of the Vukovar TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what does it -- in brief terms, what does it order the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Vukovar TO staff to do? If you can just briefly summarise.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, should I read it out? Or perhaps I should just go through it in order to better understand what the substance of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could do the latter and then perhaps just briefly summarise what the order is.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Clearing up the battle-ground. What this means is the removal of dead bodies, bodies belonging to both people and animals. It means you have to locate these bodies in a certain area. This is a task given by the commander to the 80th Motorised Brigade. And he tells them to do this in coordination with Vukovar's Territorial Defence, also in terms of accommodation, heating, logistics and reinforcements. There is mention here of 100 people to help carry the bodies. There is mention of people supposed to provide security for the teams out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Colonel, if I can stop you there, please. At paragraph 4, or paragraph 4, subparagraph 1, it states that a group of 100 men to carry out the bodily remains and the group of 10 men to provide security for the area with a team for the clearing up of battle-ground and the investigative organs will work. The investigative organs that are referred to in that order, what was their purpose, are you aware? Why were they in the area investigating and what were they investigating?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, investigative organs. Their assignment was to investigate just how and if any crimes were committed that led to murder, or to death. And to establish who was responsible. They had with them forensic specialists who were helping them with this. They did what forensic specialists usually do. They were there to make sure there was no abuse of dead bodies. And to establish responsibility. I think that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And by virtue of this order, the fact that Colonel Mrksic as Operational Group South commander is issuing it to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Territorial Defence, does that mean that the 80th Motorised Brigade were subordinate to Operational Group South command at that point in time, on the 22nd of November, by virtue of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means. Taken over the area covered by Operations Group South had to be regulated, and maybe it was for all I know, by their superior command, meaning the command of Operations Group South could by no means just cease all activity of their own free will, or leave the area without having obtained approval. There is probably a document to show that they did obtain approval, and this approval probably included such information as which unit was to take over responsibility over what used to be the area covered by Operations Group South and when, but this document is probably not available, since -- well, for the time being at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to the Territorial Defence, is it your evidence that in relation to this document, the 22nd of November, that the Vukovar Territorial Defence is still subordinated to Colonel Mrksic, the commander of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. This is a leading question. There is nothing in this order to suggest that this was committed or if this was a matter of coordination, but the witness never said that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the purpose of the question was to clarify whether it related to the Vukovar Territorial Defence. But the basis of the question, I believe, is the answer which he previously gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. In the previous answer in our version, Mr. Vasic, it's at line 25 of 68. Yes. It extends to both 80th Motorised Brigade and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on the wording of this order, it seems that the command of the 80th Brigade will regulate some issues through the staff. So this is not a matter of subordination. I believe my learned friend should have asked the colleague -- the witness as follows: Whether the TO was subordinate and not to draw conclusions based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... objection, but there is a danger that what you're doing, and it's happened on previous occasions, could reach the point of coaching the witness. Your cross-examination can deal with these issues, if necessary. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So, Witness, the question is: By virtue of this document, is it your evidence that the Vukovar Territorial Defence was still subordinated to Operational Group South as of the 22nd of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, the commander gives an assignment to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. In paragraph 4, he orders them to regulate the follows issues through the Vukovar TO staff. Territorial Defence staffs were never subordinated to any JNA units. Only TO units were, in the operations area. Therefore, what this means is that the commander is told to go to the TO staff in order to coordinate action with them. Secondly, another thing altogether is the TO units of any level. One can give orders to the TO staff, as far as command within the area of responsibility was concerned, but the commander in charge of all the activities within a certain area had under his power, command all the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can just clarify: Is a commander able to give an order to someone that is not his or -- his or her subordinate? Just in terms of military principle.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function of command defines this very clearly. A commander issues orders to subordinate units. This principle is based on -- on the principle of the function that it performs. The function of command. Some orders may be issued to officers who are not members of his unit, but only in terms of rank, function and authority, and these orders are not mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at this order on the 22nd of November, is this a mandatory order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mandatory for the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document. It's tab number 34, and the ERN number is 0463-8416 to 0463-8416, both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 424.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can now turn to tab number 35, please. And this is a combat report by Colonel Mrksic, the commander of Operational Group South zone of responsibility, to the 1st Military District command, and it's dated the 22nd of November, 1991, at 1800 hours. And in this document it states at the end of the document, if I can read out: "During the day all measures have been taken -- undertaken related to the 80th Motorised Brigade taking over the organisational and commanding functions in the area of the responsibility of operation group south. "Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade received the instructions and documents regarding the organisation of command and control in the area of responsibility of Operational Group South." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, based on this document, on the 21st of November, 1991, was the 80th Motorised Brigade still under the command of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document. It's 65 ter number 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we could now turn to tab 36, please. And this is a combat report from the Operational Group South commander, Colonel Mrksic. It's addressed to the 1st Military District and the cabinet of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and it provides a report on the situation in the area. And, again, if we look at the conclusion in the report, or the -- not the conclusion but the paragraph just above paragraph 3, it states: "All expert and organisational and material support was given to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade in resolving all issues with regards to taking over the responsibility in the area of responsibility of Operational Group South."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether, in fact, just on this document and this information in front of you, whether, in fact, the 80th Motorised Brigade had taken over the area of responsibility of Operational Group South as of the 23rd from the guards brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat again what I said earlier. This question was supposed to be resolved by the superior command, and in this document it should state exactly when the responsibility for the zone stopped for the OG and when the zone was taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade. If -- if it is stated in this report that on the 23rd all expert organisational and material support was given with regards to taking over the responsibility, it could mean that this was then the dead-line by which the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade was supposed to take over responsibility for that zone. But then again, that depends on the order that I mentioned, as to when the superior command ordered this to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that, based on this document, you are unable to say whether, in fact, responsibility had passed over to the 80th Motorised Brigade? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistance was provided on the 23rd, and all of those questions were resolved or were supposed to have been resolved. All the questions of interest for the continued functioning in the zone of the operations group. And from that point on it could have then proceeded to function. Whether that day was the day it was supposed to take over, or whether that was to be the next day, the 24th, is something that I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, in principle, Colonel, if -- whenever the date was that if the Operational Group South was taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade, in principle would Colonel Mrksic still be signing as Operational Group South commander if authority had been handed over for that zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as he is signing an order to a unit and reporting on its activities, that unit then is under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this relate to that principle of unity of command that you referred to very early in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document. It has no 65 ter number, but it's 0463-8417 to 0463-8417. Both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will be Exhibit 426.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we won't be seeking to tender the document behind paragraph [sic] 37, but there is one that has been missed by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Witness, I would ask you to turn to tab number 13, please. This is 65 ter number 931. It's a document dated the 14th of October, 1991, at 2000 hours. And it's a combat report to the 1st Military District, and it's signed buy Operational Group South commander, Colonel Mrksic. And, Witness, if I can take you to paragraph 2, it states: "In line with our order on welcoming and directing a convoy with medicine and food to Vukovar, even besides certain disapprovals and opposition by, before all others, the units of the TO, the convoy arrived safely to the Vukovar barracks." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say from your time in Vukovar whether this convoy -- or what the destination of this convoy was? It states it arrived safely at Vukovar barracks, but was it to go somewhere after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recall, this is a convoy of food and medicines sent to the population of Vukovar by the international community. Doctors Without Borders and some other international humanitarian organisations. The convoy was intended for the Croatian population. It was received and put up at the Vukovar barracks. I cannot remember what the problems were exactly that the assistance was not distributed to the population and what it was that led to the convoy being turned back. Probably it's the way it's indicated in this report, and there is a description also provided, because we could not guarantee its safety in the sections of town controlled by Ustashas. So it's probably the way that it is described here. That's probably the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how do you know that the convoy was intended for the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was intended for the Croatian population because there's an order from the 1st Military District command obliging the OG South command to regulate this matter without any obstruction. From the commander of the 1st Military District and to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know why --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I described this in the war diary too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know why the units of the TO objected and opposed to convoy?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I can make some assumptions. But I cannot really give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document. It's Rule 65 ter number 931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, the day that you left Vukovar was the 24th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Guards Motorised Brigade returned to Belgrade on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then what was your next assignment after the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the combat operations of the 19th and 20th finished, I explained to you what I did. On the 21st and the 22nd the operations and training organ, at whose head I was, was planning the return of the units from Vukovar drafting the marching plan and regulating the question of collecting or assembling the personnel and equipment in certain sectors from which we would leave. That was the task of the operations organ, and my own task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you gave your testimony yesterday that -- or maybe two days ago now, that you retired from the guards brigade as the Deputy Commander, only about a month ago, in April this year.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say how long Colonel Mrksic stayed in the Guards Motorised Brigade after returning from Vukovar? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, that was November 1991. Sometime in the autumn of 1992 he was to have formed a corps of special forces, so I think until autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Major Sljivancanin, how long did he stay in the guards brigade after the Vukovar operation, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going to lose time or waste time if I start linking things up. I can perhaps connect this, but slowly. How long he stayed in the guards brigade. He assumed the duties of Chief of Staff of the guards brigade when Panic assumed the duty of commander. So when Colonel Mrksic left, and he was a general then, to become a corps commander, the duty of Chief of Staff was assumed by Sljivancanin, also in the autumn of 1992, where he stayed for about a year, until 1993, as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And Captain Radic, are you able to say how long he stayed in the guards brigade after Vukovar, if possible?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be hard for me to answer that question too. I know that after returning from Vukovar Radic thought of leaving the army. I think that the two of us talked about that at one time. He didn't stay long, he left soon afterwards, I think. Within a year, but I really cannot be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the killings at Ovcara that occurred on the 20th to the 21st of November, 1991, were there ever any investigations conducted within the guards brigade in relation to those killings, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no. Not just an investigation, but the whole matter was not even mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to Miroljub Vujovic, a person you mentioned as being in the Vukovar TO in 1991, was he ever appointed to being the commander of the Vukovar TO, Territorial Defence? And, if he was, when was that done?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the powers of the commander of the OG South. I remember that Colonel Mrksic ordered me to write a document whereby Miroljub Vujovic was appointed as commander of the Vukovar Territorial Defence. I think that this was on the 20th at noon or in the afternoon. And I did draft that document. I don't know if it went into effect. I don't know when Colonel Mrksic signed it. I don't know if it went into effect or not. I really -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would you just excuse me for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the time, I would like your instructions. Should we take a break now and continue? Because in that case we would have an hour and 15 minutes left, so that would be a whole session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter past 3.00, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. First of all, I must ask you something. We speak the same language; therefore, can you please make a short break after each of my questions and just before you answer so that the interpreters may be given sufficient time to interpret everything, and I will myself do the same. Thank you. You testified in chief about the Law on All People's Defence. You talked about who the Supreme Commander was under the law in 1991. You said this was the president of the SFRY Presidency. What about the time of the Vukovar operation? Who was the president of the SFRY Presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I told you that it was Stipe Mesic, would that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, fair enough. That does indeed ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified that the president of the Presidency as the Supreme Commander could delegate some of its powers to the federal secretary for national defence, and in 1991 the federal secretary was Veljko Kadijevic, right? My question: Do you know that he came to that position from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is something else I want to ask you about the Law on All People's Defence. You mentioned the role and the place of Territorial Defence within the framework of All People's Defence as enshrined in the law and applying to all of the former SFRY. Do you know that based on this Law on All People's Defence there were two different kinds of structure for the TO, mobile and immobile. Unit staffs that were tied to a certain territory, and units that with the appropriate approval could have been used to carry out combat operations even outside their own territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're called, technically speaking, stationary units and manoeuvring units of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like to ask you now is to go to one of the tabs that you have in front of you. If you could please look at tab 1 in this binder; I'm talking about Exhibit 392. This is the Law on All People's Defence. If you could please go to Article 111. In the B/C/S this is page 21. In the English text, page 70.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 111, you said, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please be so kind as to read it out loud, but slowly, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commanders of the Territorial Defence and officers in charge of units and institutions of the Territorial Defence shall carry out command and control duties of the Territorial Defence in accordance with the law. "Committees for All People's Defence shall also carry out command duties in the Territorial Defence in accordance with the provisions in Article 109 of this law."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A question about what you've just read out. In carrying out their duties, did the TO commanders also -- in exercising command and control, did they also act in keeping with the instructions governing the work of the commands and staffs, what you testified about in chief, in answer to one of the questions asked by my learned friend? So, in other words, the same rules applied, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same rules applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The TO commands and staffs, did they work in keeping the rules of the instructions set out in the instructions governing the work of staffs and commands, what you testified about in chief?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as command and control were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understand, you testified in chief about the procedure of command and control and about the role of the command composition in these matters. My understanding is that under the rules the command staffs and the assistant commanders have a key role to play in terms of control. Without their role in terms of planning, organising and exercising control, the commander would never have timely information, nor would he be able to make timely decisions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please go to the brigade rules? This is tab 4; the exhibit number is 395. Please go to item 145 of this document. This is page 75 in the B/C/S and the English reference is page 44. Would you please be so kind as to read that out, item 145?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After a decision has been taken, the process of planning combat operations continues. The staff and other command organs work out in detail the use of units and produce combat documents ensuring that the decision is conveyed in full to all subordinates."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If my reading of this provision is correct, the commander first makes a decision, and this is how this decision is handed down to his subordinates. Thus ensuring, in detail, how the units mentioned in the order are used, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, first you have to do the planning bit from item 145. Conveying the order is something different. That is enshrined in item 146, but what you say is accurate. The planning bit is done by organs of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please go back to the Law on All People's Defence at tab 1. The exhibit number is 392. Please go to Article 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Indeed. This is page 21 in the B/C/S, page 72 in the English. Please be so kind as to read that out for us.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army and units and institutions of the Territorial Defence involved in a joint combat operation shall be subordinated to the officer in charge of carrying out the operation. "In temporarily occupied territory, when required by the combat situations, commanders of the Territorial Defence shall also assume command and control over units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army, unless otherwise stipulated by plans or special orders. "Territorial Defence staffs shall coordinate any plans and combat activities of the Territorial Defence with the plans and combat activities of the Yugoslav People's Army, as well as with any plans and activities of the Territorial Defence of the neighbouring socio-political community."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now please go to the provisions under Article 114 of the Law on All People's Defence. It's the same page.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Territorial Defence commanders shall also be responsible for their work, combat readiness and command of the Territorial Defence to the competent organs in socio-political communities. Territorial Defence commanders shall also be responsible for their work, combat readiness and use and command of the Territorial Defence in temporarily occupied territories to the organ in charge of all people's resistance in those territories. Officers in charge of use of units and/or institutions shall also be responsible for their work, combat readiness and command of Territorial Defence units and institutions within organisations of associated labour and local communes to the governing bodies of such organisations and/or the relevant bodies in local communes."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All these provisions were in force back in 1991 when the combat operations in Vukovar were taking place, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief about the fact that operative and tactical groups could be created within a corps as well as tactical groups. Can we then agree that these units are units established within the composition of a corps? What about their composition? Is that inferior or superior to a corps, because I think that's what the rule states, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is there not a rule that when an operative or tactical group is set up, which may have several different brigades and other brigade-level units within its composition, that a special command is set up, or that the command of a unit is strengthened up to the required level, so that this temporary or provisional military unit may be able to effectively perform its duty, or, rather, in order to ensure that command and control are exercised in a satisfactory manner. In view of the fact that an operative tactical group, as a unit, has a much wider scope than the original unit, for example, a brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. If you take into account that establishment command does not have the required capacity to exercise command in terms of its manpower, or anything else, well, then, what is usually done is it is reinforced by the superior command or from a different source.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If an operative tactical group comprises several brigades, is it then the case that the command of one brigade has sufficient manpower in its command as to be able to exercise command over such a large unit as an operative tactical group?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes that is the case, and sometimes that is not the case. It depends. In this specific case, the command of the guards brigade was -- had the capacity in terms of its manpower to take over command. And the superior commander probably bore that in mind when making his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as the command of the guards brigade is concerned, and that is what you have just mentioned, this became part of Operations Group South, right? You said you believed them to be -- to have the required capacity in terms of manpower. What about the guards brigade before it became a part of Operations Group South? Did it have a separate command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I think -- I think they did, but its capacity or ability was rather poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that Colonel Bajo Bojat, as commander of Operations Group South, when giving the order to establish this group, actually obtained a special command, the command of Operations Group South. It wasn't the fact that the Mitrovica [as interpreted] brigade command was turned into the command of the Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but the situation on the ground when I came was such that my impression was that the command had next to no capacity at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. You will agree with me that when the commander of the guards brigade was transformed into the commander of Operations Group South received no reinforcements whatsoever. In actual fact, the commander of one brigade at this point in time became the command of a unit which comprised several brigades, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me this, please: My learned friend asked you about your arrival in the guards brigade. My apologies, there is intervention for the transcript, page 85, line 3. I was talking about the command of the Sremska Mitrovica brigade, whereas the transcript only says the Mitrovica command. Thank you. Now, to go back to my question. Can you tell us what was the ethnic make-up of the guards brigade before its being sent to the Vukovar war zone as regards both rank and file?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people there of various ethnicities. In my assessment, as regards the soldiers, some 20 per cent of them were Croatian. As regards the officers, a quota was used. Irrespective of the criteria, based on which officers were assigned to the guards brigade, those criteria were quite harsh and the quota used was the percentage of the representation of various ethnic groups within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the quotas needed to be respected at the time, as prescribed by law, and all organs had to abide by that, not only the socio-political communities, but some control was also exercised by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the quota, they were defined by the General Staff, that is the Federal Secretariat, based on the ethnic make-up in the country. And the criteria prescribed had to be met. When it refers to the soldiers the criteria was very harsh. It depended on some security checks, on the physical prowess, as well as some other characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since we are a discussing the criteria on the composition of the unit, am I right in saying that the officer cadre in the guards brigade during the relevant period, that is when they were deployed in Vukovar, was of different ethnic make-up, and the -- their aim was to preserve the all-Yugoslav nature of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would again reiterate that you should pause before you answer, because interpreters have difficulty catching up; hence, we could omit a part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We talked about the principle abided by the officers of the guards brigade to try and preserve the unity of the SFRY. Did they base that on the then constitution and the Law on All People's Defence, which encompassed the obligation of the JNA to preserve the integrity of the country?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm this for me: When you were sent to the Vukovar front, was your primary task to deblock the barracks of the JNA in Vukovar and then to put into practice the decision by the Supreme Command and the Presidency of the SFRY to disarm the paramilitary Croatian formations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be quite precise as regards that, but the first decision, I believe, concerned the deblocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before your arrival at the area of Vukovar, were you familiar with the fact that there was an attempt to deblock the barracks in the centre of town, which failed, as well as the first action undertaken by the guards brigade at the beginning of October?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief what was the role and position of the guards brigade. You said it was directly subordinated to the chef de cabinet of the Federal Secretariat for National defence, Mr. Vuk Obradovic. Does that mean that the tasks, prior to the brigade being sent to Vukovar, were given by the chef de cabinet on behalf of the federal secretary, and at that time was the brigade reporting on a daily basis to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until the moment when the order regulated its subordination to the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as we could see from the reports shown to you by my learned friend, even after the resubordination to the 1st Military District, the reports were being sent both to the military district and to the Federal Secretariat as regards the actions the guards brigade undertook within OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was reported to two various organs, one of them being the chef de cabinet of the federal secretary. We were told to report to them as well; therefore, we sent reports to two various addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in chief you mentioned that decision by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence by which the guards brigade was resubordinated to the 1st Military District before being sent to the Vukovar front. Once there, you told us that by decision of the 1st Military District commander it was then resubordinated to Operations Group South. Could we please have an order on the screen, and then I will ask for your clarification. It is number 0D00-0426 in the B/C/S. In the English it is 0D00-0427. I would kindly ask the usher to give this to the witness. Perhaps it would be easier for the witness to have that in the hard copy. I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is all the same to me when I put my glasses on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, the -- I just wanted to say that this is a guards command -- guards brigade command order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the date and the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You can see the report. It states there that the Guards Motorised Brigade, based on the orders of the 1st Military District, was being resubordinated to the 12th Corps in order to carry out a task.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the guards brigade was first resubordinated to the 12th Corps and then to Operations Group South, which fell under the 12th Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how we should read what it states here, yes. As to why, I presume the 12th Corps coordinated the entire operation of liberation of Vukovar before splitting into two operation zones, that of the north and the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the 12th Corps commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what his name was, but I believe that he was killed on Trpinjska Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
