utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have the number in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is 0D00-0427.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 428.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in chief you explained how the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade came to the area of Vukovar on the 30th of September, 1991. And in the war diary for the 18th of October, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, for the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It was then renamed the command of the Operations Group South within which the guards brigade fell. You also stated that the command post of Operations Group South was at Negoslavci. Could you confirm for me whether at Negoslavci at the time there was the command post as well as the assistance or replacement command post in the village of Berak?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the guards brigade became part of Operations Group South and after the command of the brigade became the command of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the command post was at Negoslavci, but it wasn't an auxiliary command post, but rather the forward command post in one part of Negoslavci, and there was the rear command post in the village of Berak that was transferred there from the area of Vibarac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know which command organs were at the respective command post, at which command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff was at the command post without its morale organ, which was at the rear command post. Also, without a part of the personnel organ, which was also at the rear command post. A few people from the security organ, one or two men, were also at the rear command post. And the service units and the communications units were at the command post, as well as the entire staff, including the operatives, the heads, the personnel assistants and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was then at the forward command post at Negoslavci? At the time of the tasks being carried out, were there security organs there, as well as the assistant for morale and the detention for soldiers, as well as the team for criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post operated as of our arrival to Vukovar, Colonel Bajo Bojat was there, and the post was in the northern part of Negoslavci. The brigade command was in the centre of Negoslavci in the house I mentioned. As for the forward command post, depending on the situation and the actions, people went there, various people. The commander was there often, as well as the Chief of Staff, then some people from the operations organs, as well as from various branches of the armed forces. It was used depending on the dynamics of the operation. That's precisely why it was called forward, in order to provide better management ability to the command. But the basic command post was in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in chief you've described the operations room where you worked. Was it at the main command post, or at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the main command post. Or to be precise, once command was taken over of OG South, the following two days the command moved to the main command post while the forward command post ceased to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there a place in Negoslavci where the assistant for morale, security, criminal investigations, were located? Was that part of the command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post is a broader term. I concluded that it was unconditional in order to set up all the elements of the command post, as is provided under regulations. Thus, the operations group at the command post was in the operations room. The auxiliary group you're mentioning, the morale and personnel organs, were in another house also in the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the security organs, military prison, and the morale sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said well, some of them were in the same house where the main group was. This was just a part, maybe one or two of the officers, not all of them. Some of them were at the rear command post, and some were at the auxiliary main or auxiliary basic command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to ask you, with the help of the usher, if you recall, and I assume that you recall because you answered a question by my learned friend about that, to sketch the premises of this main command post, where the commander was and where the operations room was. Thank you. We're talking about the command post where the operations room was, where the commander slept, and also the place where you carried out your duties.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. As far as I remember, it looked like this. I cannot sketch the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, all I'm interested in is the layout of the rooms, not the actual building. What I would like to ask you is to mark the operations room. Actually, let's start from the entrance. Could you please mark the entrance with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please mark the operations room with number 2.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This part in the operations room that is marked with CV, if I understand you correctly, that is the communications centre. Could you mark that with the number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The room that is marked the room for the commander's rest, could you please mark that with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The next room is the room for the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with number 5.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then we have the work room. Could you please mark that with number 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then the office for general affairs, could you please mark that with number 7.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since we are looking at the sketch now, could you please tell us where the desk or table was where meetings were being held and where the operational part of the command was functioning?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large desk in the middle of the room, and then there were two or three smaller desks arranged next to the wall. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So these small rectangles, you could mark them all with the number 8, and that's one large desk in the centre and smaller desks arranged around the room.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Yes, there were several desks, I'm marking them with the number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with number 9 the place where the commander sat in the operations room when he was there.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was holding meetings then he would sit at the head of the large table.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with a 9.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. And when he was just monitoring the situation, then he was somewhere near the communications centre, perhaps to the side somewhere. There was an exit there. I marked the main entrance with number 1, and there was an auxiliary exit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with the number 10, the auxiliary exit.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where the commander sat when he was monitoring the work?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was holding meetings and briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You marked that with the number 9, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right next to his room for rest, that's where it was. I think opposite from the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with number 11.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the duty operations officer, did he have a permanent place somewhere in this room?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one of these three desks. Two or three desks. Two or three. Maybe there were not three; maybe there were two. But he did have one of those desks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with the number 12 the desk used by the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to mark it. I cannot remember which of those desks it was. It's been 15 years since then. I am managing to remember documents but not able to remember the desks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's not so important which one it was. I just wanted all of us to have an idea of where everything was.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you can consider that I have not been able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me: When somebody entered the command, were they obliged to announce themselves, somebody from outside of the command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had to report to the duty operations officer. Also, in the basement there was a restaurant and a kitchen. That's where you would go to eat. So everybody would pass through the room in order to go downstairs to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you remember where this entrance was that led to the basement? Could you indicate this on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I cannot. Somewhere near the exit, the auxiliary exit. That's where you would go down -- down to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether this building had more than one floor, and if it did, what was upstairs?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. The man was in Novi Sad, he allowed us to use the room -- the building. It had perhaps one or two rooms upstairs and a balcony, but that was really small.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me where the commander slept when he wasn't in the operations room or in that room in the command, when he wasn't in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in the room for the rest of the commander, that's where he would sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's at the same level as the operations room?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you just please draw the road or the street, what side it was on, and could you please indicate the direction that Vukovar is in so that we roughly get the idea of the position of the -- of the house?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. This is south, and this is north.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this diagram --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this diagram will become Exhibit 429.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You replied earlier to a question by the Prosecutor about the daily briefings in OG South and that they were held in the operations room. And could you please tell us whether this was from between 1700 to 1800 hours, because we saw that regular combat reports were sent to the superior command, the 1st Military District, and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was most often held at 1700 hours. And there were cases sometimes when there were briefings in the morning, sometime at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us who attended the briefings, so we will not repeat that. What I would like to know is if you can tell us where the important details from these briefings were noted, such as reports by commanders of subordinate units or commander's orders or the report on the situation of the field in the units, was this recorded anywhere in a special briefings book?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a book, briefings book. It was written by one of the operations officers. I can't remember which one. Yes, these briefings were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this was a separate log from the document that we've already seen the -- the war diary and also the register of documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this document also kept like other documents from the brigade command, just like the register of documents, the war diary? Were they also kept in the operations room, and when others were absent were they in the care of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the briefings book was in the keeping of the officer who actually wrote down entries in the book. But it was on the desk. There were no possibilities of specially securing the book or guarding it in any special way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the names of the operations officers in the OG command, OG South command, if you remember them?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember them. Major Gojkovic, Major Skoric, Samo Kokol. Samo Kokol, a Slovenian. And two others, but I'm tired now, and I really cannot remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These officers, one of them was the operations duty officer every day. They worked in shifts, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they worked in shifts, but -- perhaps I should wait if you want that question. The duty officers were taken from the list of those on duties, so all the staff officers were included in this duty roster from all the branches, from the personnel organ. All those who were at the command post from the morale organ. There was a group of 14 of them in shifts of seven days' duration. We would change on every seventh day, that's when the shifts would be relieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you were working in shifts, does that mean that there were three officers on duty per day working eight hours, or was this done in a different way?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you exactly. In the beginning it was organised that there would be half and half within the shift, and the shift leader would tell us when to rest. Later we worked out a roster of duty so that you would have classic duties, the duty officer and his assistant, and it would be from midnight until the morning. So both of these options were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And anyone who wanted to reach the commander or the Chief of Staff or any other person from the command organ had to report to the duty officer. Was that the rule?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that rule was not respected. It was -- everything was at such a pace that the senior officer would come, I mean they're not really very high ranks, lieutenant-colonels and so on, and they would come and say, lieutenant, sir, such-and-such a thing. So procedures had to be left aside. Because everything was happening. So quickly it was all happening in one place. Perhaps if there was a special room for the work of the duty officer, then perhaps we could have respected these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How was anyone to know whether any head of an organ or the commander were free to see him?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another issue. The commander was there almost all the time. Or he could be in his rest room. In his absence the officers, based on the information that he was to be told, would decide whether to invite him to come to the operations room or not. But since he was there most of the time, it was quite simple. People reported to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, the duty officer decided whether he would have to inform the commander, whether he would disturb his rest?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: To go back to the briefing we discussed, upon completion of any given briefing, regular combat reports were drafted and sent to the superior commands reflecting the information explained at the briefing and pertaining to the relevant period of time. That is, from 1800 hours on the previous day until the 1800 hours on the day of the sending of the report?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation as may have changed since the last report, but the briefings were not on a daily basis. Reports were compiled based on information received by the operations duty officer, and the data you saw in the war diary came via reports of the subordinates or various command organs that were out in the field. When there was no briefing, that was the way to draft the report. And the commander would then go through the report in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And once he would go through it, he would sign it, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He would also ask for certain corrections to be made, if necessary. But once he would sign it, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And after having read and signed the report, how was it forwarded to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was delivered to the general affairs office, and I don't know what procedure they followed. They filed reports and then forwarded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As regards the sketch you made of the command post, you marked the communications centre there, how did it work, and whether there was any communication with the superior units being the command of the 1st Military District and the cabinet of the federal secretary?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Communications centre is something that encompasses usually more than what we had. We only had a portion of it. But to your answer, I would reply with a yes. We communicated with both our subordinate and superior units, as well as with the cabinet of the federal secretary and the 1st Military District command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify for us what were the tasks and the role of the duty operations officer as regards his daily and night-time tasks, once he would be left there alone?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was there by himself, his tasks were clear. He was responsible for order and regular work in the operations room. He was also responsible to receive information to assess their importance. Since the commander was right there, if he thought them to be important, he would notify the commander. If not, he would note them down and report them to the commander the next morning. He also was to inform the operations organ, and then those -- that information was also entered into the war diary as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During -- or at day-time, were his tasks any different while everyone was at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His tasks were different. The commander is there, as well as the Chief of Staff, and maybe the head of the operations organ. Orders are being received via telephone, and at the communications centre there was a radio man who had a form, although it wasn't an official document, and he would receive reports, usually coded ones. He would decode them and inform the duty officer or the operations officer or the commander, if there was no one at hand to receive that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I believe in your testimony in chief you stated that the war diary that you kept, overnight was with the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was with him in the operations room at all times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we look at the documents it becomes clear that combat actions took place at day-time, if I'm not mistaken. Could you tell me when the command staff would go and rest? I believe that depended on a given day.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around midnight. I usually left around midnight, provided I wasn't the duty officer or if I wasn't ordered to do the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the war diary was kept in the operations room with the duty officer, in the morning when you returned did you control the entries, or was the duty officer there to inform you of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He noted down the information, and once I got there then the entries were made into the war diary. He noted them down before that in his notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's already 4.30. I don't know whether I can see the clock properly from my -- from where I am standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With a little imagination, it's 4.30, Mr. Vasic. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
